source: It is a delicate balance of power. And there are some within Elsinore who would prefer to tip the whole scale.
Yes, I suspect that there will be those within Elsinore who are your true enemies. They will make their faces known to you soon.
Women understand subtlety and statesmanship. Men understand only how to rule by force and fear. Do not let fools in Elsinore run your country.
I see. Fascinating.
Irma, I'm sorry I have kept you at arm's length these years. It's clear I have much to learn from you.
I'm sure I will be coming to you for advice in the future as well.
Good luck. May you be twice the man your uncle was.
Heard you were looking for encouragement, so I came to find you.
You more than anyone else, my friend.
What advice do you have for me?
More warnings than wisdoms, unfortunately.
I fought beside your father when he went to war. I saw the way he rallied the Danish nobility to his cause.
And... then... I witnessed your uncle cast them aside, leaving them angry and unsettled. He pretended they didn't exist.
Currently, a great deal of them are quite angry. At you. And it will fall to your shoulders to settle their hearts.
Do you think you're up to the task?
I... don't know. I think so.
It feels like I've inherited a court full of men who hate and fear me.
Perhaps if you can assuage the enemies outside your court, you can deal with the ones within.
Enemies within? Who do you mean?
You know well enough who I mean. Who has treated you with stable revulsion for years? Who has claim to the throne?
Aye. And he'll not be thrilled to hear you've taken your uncle's seat.
Are you saying I... must... be rid of him?
He's Ophelia's brother. Though I bear him no great love, it would tear her apart to lose him.
Being a King involves making hard decisions. Decisions you know may hurt the ones you love.
Laertes is a decision you must make.
Were I in your place, he'd be gone by nightfall.
You've given me much to consider. Thanks, friend, as always.
Love, I heard you were looking for advice.
I was.
Hamlet. I know you still hold me in revulsion.
And I cannot change that, nor can I soften your heart.
Actually, Mother, I believe I owe you an apology.
I have been devastatingly cruel to you, I'm afraid.
I've treated you in ways no son should treat his mother.
You are Denmark's Dowager-Queen. For now, we rule together. Mother and son.
You don't know how long I've desperately wanted to hear you say that.
My child. My little love. I'm so sorry. Everything that's transpired...
Some moments I think the events of the last few months have all been one terrible dream.
Then think of them that way. I certainly do.
Oh. You wanted advice. Please excuse me.
You have already acted on the best advice I might give-- to marry well, and quickly.
I know it can't have been easy, but your union with Lady Brit will prove a strong one for Denmark.
Then what a simple matter it is to receive such advice.
Look at you. Your whole demeanor has changed. There's something new in you.
And something familiar. Something beloved.
You are going to make a fine King.
I saw you escorting Ophelia to your chambers.
Ah. Mother.
If there is one good word I can give to you, it is to marry well, and marry carefully.
The nobles will call a vote to determine whether you may truly be their King when you take the throne.
At that time, if they dislike you, it will come to war, or worse. You will be ousted, and all of us will be forced from Elsinore.
But if you can select a suitable marriage which appeases the nobility, then such a crisis could be avoided.
Luckily, there is one obvious candidate here at court for that very reason. I had hoped to make peace between all parties.
You mean Brit?
If you were to marry Brit, it would be an alliance between Denmark's crown and her nobility.
We had hoped to make such a match with Lady Brit, of course. But no longer. Still--
If you were to marry the daughter of a Danish noble house, it would be an alliance between Denmark's crown and her nobility.
And all would be at peace.
But I don't think I can make that promise.
There's someone else.
I know. I know you love her. But listen to me.
In my long years of reign I have learned but one thing to be forever true.
We do not rule for our own desires. Our hearts must live outside us, on public display.
If you marry Ophelia, peace will be hard won. Brit's family will see it as a rejection of the impending betrothal we had planned.
And that will make your work in the future all the more difficult.
Out of love, I beg you to reconsider asking for Ophelia's hand, and to marry Brit instead.
If you marry Ophelia, peace will be hard won. The nobility will see it as a rejection of all other options.
I love Ophelia.
But I have lived selfishly a long time. I cannot live just for myself anymore. Not now.
Besides, she's made it very clear that she doesn't return my feelings. I should respect that.
Perhaps you're right. Perhaps there's truth in what you say.
I will think on it. I can promise that much. Thank you, Mother.
I do not say these things to cause you pain. Merely to help you be the best King you can be.
I love you, Hamlet. Regardless of what I say, I know you'll make a choice all your own, and be the wiser for it.
Hamlet! Why, we've been informed you're looking for a sage's word.
We're the smartest people we know, so of course we wanted to help.
Is it true that you'll be ascending to your uncle's throne?
Not just yet. But in the future... God willing, yes.
But Hamlet, you've never been the type to sit in a room all day and hand out judgements.
It does seem a little out of character.
Won't you be bored? Won't you come to hate your duties as soon as you take them up?
What Guilda is impolitely moving towards... is... an invitation, Hamlet. To join us.
Come back to Wittenberg with us. Let some other fool run the country!
What she means is, you needn't take the crown unless you feel it would truly bring you happiness.
Entertainment is not one of my concerns. This is my country. These are my people. And with my uncle and father gone...
Denmark's back is bare, and she is exposed to any who would drive a stake through her.
Hamlet, we know that in light of your uncle's death, you feel a great sense of duty to your country. That is noble-hearted.
But you've been through much lately, all of it difficult and straining. It has taken a great toll on you.
If this isn't something that will make you happy, is it worth throwing your life away for?
Do you want to be King? Weren't you telling us just yesterday how much you wanted to sail away and never return?
All this has been so fast. What I wanted didn't factor into my thinking.
Perhaps a man who has the kinds of thoughts I've had isn't the best man to rule Denmark after all.
Perhaps my doubts unmake me. Certainly my father never had them.
We just want what's best for you, Hamlet, and your happiness.
We leave soon. If you care to journey with us, you're more than welcome.
You've given me much to think about. Thank you, Rosie, Guilda.
(Seems like that advice wasn't useful at all. I'm not sure what I expected.)
My prince! Heard yeh were lookin' for advice earlier.
So! Yer goin' to seat the throne after all, eh?
Well. As th' oldest serving guard in the castle, I've seen me a lot a' trouble in my day.
An' all of it stems from those blasted nobles! They're never happy. Weren't with yer father, weren't with yer uncle...
I think it's high time we crushed 'em beneath our boots!
You'd have us go to war with them? Truly?
They don' respond to threats, bribery, peace talks, or any other strategy... what's left?
To hell with 'em. All of 'em. And may Denmark long rule!
I see. Thank you, Marcellus.
Perhaps there is no way forward with the nobility which involves peace.
Perhaps shows of force are all they respect.
(That's terrible advice. I expected better of Marcellus.)
(If Brit's family is working with Fortinbras against us, then we've no hope of attacking our own nobility. Not that we'd even want to.)
(I wonder if there's anyone who can encourage Hamlet to form an alliance instead.)
My lord. How is your state of mind?
Better than it's been in a long time. What can I do for you, sir?
Oh ho! It's been a long time since you addressed me with any form of title. Well, then.
I've come to offer you a little advice. I'm sure other men and women can offer you better words on matters going on outside the castle.
The nobility is a problem you must solve. How you do so is up to you. But I come here to warn you about something more formidable.
There are always going to be enemies within your own walls.
Something I wish your father had known deeply was that any man can be driven by jealousy to commit foul deeds.
Rid yourself of enemies at court, and you will live harmoniously, young Prince. I promise it.
Enemies at court? You mean here, in Elsinore?
Ah, but who would want me dead? I can only--
Y-you're right, Polonius. I can't believe I was so blind.
Of course there will need to be a purging when I become King.
Anyone within a King's court understands the need for privacy and safety, my lord. None will be offended.
Just, please, don't wait. I wish every day your father were still with us. Had we been more prudent then, he might have been.
Thank you for the advice, Polonius. I'll think on it.
Very well.
Bernardo, give the ready signal. Our dispatch will ride ahead shortly.
Yes, my lord. All is at attention here.
Marcellus, are the men in town ready to move forth?
Aye, all that I kin see.
Good. Then let's go.
Hamlet, where are you going?
I'm leaving to visit the countryside.
I didn't anticipate we'd go so soon, of course.
Are you sure this is wise?
It is what's best. We intend to make a small show of force to shake the nobility.
Nothing extreme. Hamlet will be in the care of the best men I can offer him.
Marcellus and I will be staying behind to maintain security at home while Hamlet is away.
And what if he doesn't return?
I have full faith in Bernardo on this matter.
